title: Epidemiological data analysis for babies
text:
Preface
A model is a simplified representation of a complex phenomenon (Vynnycky & White, 2010), focusing on key factors and making simplifying assumptions. These assumptions must be valid for the model to be accurate.
How do we know if an assumption holds true? Assumptions act as our hypotheses, which we can test by analysing the data. This book guides you through the methods and visualisations to validate assumptions in epidemiological models.




Vynnycky, E., & White, R. (2010). An Introduction to Infectious Disease Modelling. OUP Oxford.

title: 1  Age distribution
1  Age distribution
text:
1.2 Time series stacked bar
We want to see if the age distribution changes during the epidemic. The age categories are in age_cat, and we will look at how they change weekly. First, we will group the onset days into weeks using floor_date() from the lubridate package.

df$week_onset <- floor_date(df$date_onset, "week")

Compute the weekly percentage for each group.

df_plot <- df |> 
  filter(!is.na(week_onset), !is.na(age_cat)) |> 
  count(week_onset, age_cat) |> 
  group_by(week_onset) |> 
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |> 
  data.frame()

# Use complete() to fill missing groups with 0
df_plot <- df_plot |> 
  complete(week_onset, age_cat, fill = list(n = 0, prop = 0))

Plot it with geom_bar().

ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = week_onset, y = prop, fill = age_cat)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_jco() +
  theme_minimal()








You might want to reverse the order so that ages 0-4 are at the bottom and 70+ at the top. Do this by setting the position argument. Also, reverse the legend to match the new plot order.

ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = week_onset, y = prop, fill = age_cat)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  scale_fill_jco() +
  theme_minimal()

title: 2  Seroprevalence
text:
2.1 Imperfect test
Recall how to compute sensitivity and specificity:

title: 2  Seroprevalence
text:
Disease (D)
Control (C)




Positive (P)
True positive (TP)
False positive (FP)


Negative (N)
False negative (FN)
True negative (TN)



\[\begin{align}\text{Sensitivity} &= \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{Disease}} \\ &= \mathbb{P}(P|D)\end{align}\]
\[\begin{align} \text{Specificity} &= \frac{\text{TN}}{\text{Control}} \\ &= \mathbb{P}(N|C) \end{align}\]




2.1.1 Rogan-Gladen correction
Let:

\(\pi_{est}\): the prevalence estimated from data with confidence interval \((a, b)\).
\(\pi_{true}\): the true prevalence with confidence interval \((c, d)\).
Sensitivity (\(SE\)) and specificity (\(SP\)) are known.

\[\begin{align}
\pi_{est} &= \frac{\text{positive}}{\text{total}} = \frac{TP + FP}{\text{total}} = \frac{TP}{\text{total}} + \frac{FP}{\text{total}} \\
&= \frac{\text{disease}}{\text{total}} \times \frac{TP}{\text{disease}} + \frac{\text{control}}{\text{total}} \times \frac{FP}{\text{control}} \\
&= \frac{\text{disease}}{\text{total}} \times \frac{TP}{\text{disease}} + \frac{\text{control}}{\text{total}} \times (1 - \frac{TN}{\text{control}}) \\
&= \pi_{true} \times SE + (1 - \pi_{true}) \times (1 - SP) \\
&= \pi_{true} \times SE + 1 - SP - \pi_{true} \times (1 - SP) \\
&= \pi_{true} \times (SE + SP - 1) + 1 - SP
\end{align}\]






Bayesian derivation





\[\begin{align}
\pi_{est} &= \mathbb{P}(P) = \mathbb{P}(P \cap D) + \mathbb{P}(P \cap C) \\
&= \mathbb{P}(P|D) \times \mathbb{P}(D) + \mathbb{P}(P|C) \times \mathbb{P}(C) \\
&= SE \times \pi_{true} + (1 - SP) \times (1 - \pi_{true})
\end{align}\]



(Rogan & Gladen, 1978) derive \(\pi_{true}\) as:
\[\pi_{true} = \frac{\pi_{est} + SP - 1}{SE + SP - 1}\]
Confidence interval of the true prevalence \((c, d)\) can be estimated by many methods:

(Diggle, 2011) suggested a simple transformation:

\[\begin{align}
c &= \text{max}(0, \frac{a + SP - 1}{SE + SP - 1}) \\
d &= \text{min}(1, \frac{b + SP - 1}{SE + SP - 1})
\end{align}\]


2.1.2 Bayesian correction




Diggle, P. J. (2011). Estimating Prevalence Using an Imperfect Test. Epidemiology Research International, 2011(1), 608719. https://doi.org/10.1155/2011/608719


Rogan, W. J., & Gladen, B. (1978). Estimating prevalence from the results of a screening test. American Journal of Epidemiology, 107(1), 71–76. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a112510

title: 3  Relative measures
text:
Intervention
Control




Event
A
B


Non-event
C
D



\[Risk_{int} = \frac{A}{A + C}\]
\[Risk_{ctrl} = \frac{B}{B + D}\]



\[Odds_{int}= \frac{A}{C}\]
\[Odds_{ctrl}= \frac{B}{D}\]



Let see the \(Risk\) formula:
\[\begin{align}
Risk_{int} &= \frac{A}{A + C} \\
&= \frac{\frac{A}{C}}{\frac{A + C}{C}} = \frac{\frac{A}{C}}{\frac{A}{C} + 1} \\
&= \frac{Odds_{int}}{Odds_{int} + 1}
\end{align}\]
So \(Risk \approx Odds\) when \(Odds + 1 \approx 1\), which is when \(Odds \approx 0\). This is why people often say the odds ratio (OR) and risk ratio (RR) are interchangeable when the baseline risk is very low, meaning the outcome is rare. When the risk falls below 20%, odds and risk become more similar, and they are nearly identical when the risk is below 10% (Darzi et al., 2023).




Darzi, A. J., Busse, J. W., Phillips, M., Wykoff, C. C., Guymer, R. H., Thabane, L., Bhandari, M., & Chaudhary, V. (2023). Interpreting results from randomized controlled trials: What measures to focus on in clinical practice. Eye, 37(15), 3055–3058. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-023-02454-7

title: 4  Advanced visualisation
text:
4.1 Font family
install.packages("systemfonts")
Use systemfonts::system_fonts() to manage the fonts installed on your computer.
systemfonts::system_fonts() |> View()
If it’s a google font: Navigate to Google Fonts > Search > Download > Unzip the file > Select all the .ttf files > Right click and select Install. R tends to play nicer with .ttf fonts than other types of fonts.
After installing, go to Session > Restart R > Use systemfonts::system_fonts() |> View() to search the font. If it’s there, you are safe to use.
Set the graphics device to AGG. Tools > Global options > General > Graphics > Backend: AGG.
Set the graphics device at the start of your Quarto file.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, dev = "ragg_png", dpi = 400)
Let’s try an example.
Code
p1 <- trees |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = Girth,
    y = Height,
    size = Volume,
    colour = Volume
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Nunito Sans") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(text = element_text(family = "Nunito Sans"), legend.position = "none")
p2 <- trees |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = Girth,
    y = Height,
    size = Volume,
    colour = Volume
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Karla") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(text = element_text(family = "Karla"), legend.position = "none")
p1 | p2
